filaments.name: ABS (Acrylonitrile Butadiene Styrene)
filaments.summary: The classic engineering thermoplastic: tough, impact-resistant, usable near 95-100 °C and uniquely acetone-smoothable. In exchange it is the hardest of the commodity three to print — high shrinkage, real warping and delamination without a heated enclosure, poor UV life, and styrene fumes that demand ventilation.

price.notes: 2025-2026 pricing for standard unfilled grades: budget $18-22, mid $20-24, premium $28-35 per kg. ABS no longer undercuts PETG — budget PETG now often matches or beats it.

recommended: cosmetic parts finished by acetone vapour smoothing
parts needing higher HDT than PLA or PETG
snap-fit and interlocking assemblies (good fatigue resistance)
prototypes intended for sanding and painting
not_recommended: UV-exposed outdoor parts (yellows and embrittles — use ASA instead)
food-contact items
printing in an unventilated occupied room (styrene fumes)
open-frame printers or beginners (warping and delamination)
fine-detail miniatures
storage or use in humid conditions without drying

filaments.name: ASA (Acrylonitrile Styrene Acrylate)
filaments.summary: ABS reformulated for sunlight: the same styrenic stiffness, impact resistance and ~100 °C glass transition, but with a weather-stable acrylate rubber phase that makes it the best UV and outdoor performer among common filaments. The cost is ABS-grade warping that demands an enclosure, and high styrene-dominated emissions that demand ventilation.

price.notes: 2025-2026 pricing for standard unfilled grades: budget brands ~$18-22, Bambu $29.99/kg, premium Prusament/Polymaker and specialty colours ~$35-45 per kg. Exact bounds unverified.

recommended: automotive exterior trim and license-plate frames
mailboxes and other permanently sun-exposed housings
drone and RC frames exposed to sun
not_recommended: food-contact items
indoor decor where PLA would do the job more easily
printing in unenclosed, unventilated occupied rooms (styrene VOCs)
tight-tolerance small parts printed without an enclosure (corner lift and warp)
flexible or energy-absorbing applications needing elastomer behaviour

filaments.name: BVOH (Butenediol Vinyl Alcohol Copolymer)
filaments.summary: The premium water-soluble support material: it dissolves faster and prints more stably than PVA, holds up over multi-day dual-material jobs, and pairs cleanly with PETG, ASA, nylon and even TPU where PVA struggles. The trade-offs are cost — often two to three times PVA — and the same extreme hygroscopy in storage.

price.notes: Premium-priced and consistently more expensive than PVA across sources, reflecting more complex chemistry. Direct retail data point: Fiberlogy BVOH 0.5 kg at EUR 86.47 incl. VAT (roughly $95 for the spool at recent rates), implying about $150-250/kg. The per-kg USD figure is converted and estimated (unverified) — no direct USD retail listing was found.

recommended: dissolvable supports for PETG (better than PVA here per Prusa and BCN3D)
supports for ASA and other engineering filaments
supports for nylon and high-temperature blends
complex overhangs and internal channels where clean dissolution and surface quality matter
multi-day dual-material prints needing better stability than PVA
supports for flexible materials such as TPU 98A
not_recommended: standalone functional parts (dissolves in water, not load-bearing)
food-contact parts
outdoor or humid-exposure parts
budget-constrained short or simple prints where PVA's lower cost is adequate

filaments.name: HIPS (High Impact Polystyrene)
filaments.summary: A light, styrenic material with two lives: a limonene-dissolvable support material and a genuinely usable lightweight build material for props, prototypes and RC airframes. It prints in the ABS difficulty tier — enclosure, warm bed, minimal part cooling — but shrinks noticeably less than ABS and sands and vapour-smooths beautifully.

price.notes: 2025-2026 pricing for standard unfilled grades (3DSourced). Observed retail: 3DXTech 3DXMAX HIPS around $32/kg, MatterHackers around $36-43/kg for 1 kg spools with bulk discounts.

recommended: limonene-dissolvable support material (traditionally paired with ABS)
cosplay props and helmets (low density keeps wearables light)
RC aircraft and drone airframe components
architectural models needing fine sanding or machining
parts finished by chemical vapour smoothing (limonene or acetone)
not_recommended: outdoor or UV-exposed parts (no UV stabiliser; embrittles and yellows)
direct repeated food contact
parts needing high surface hardness (scratches easily)
fire-sensitive applications (flammable, releases styrene fumes)
precision parts needing minimal shrink and warp without an enclosure

filaments.name: PA (Nylon / Polyamide)
filaments.summary: The toughest common engineering filament: outstanding layer adhesion, wear and impact resistance, and low friction, which is why it dominates gears, bushings and living mechanical parts. It is also the most demanding material here — extremely hygroscopic, high-warping, and dimensionally restless as humidity changes, so it needs constant drying, an enclosure and a forgiving build surface.

price.notes: 2025-2026 unfilled PA6/PA12 pricing extrapolated from observed spool prices: budget eSUN lines ~$30-40/kg, Polymaker PolyMide CoPA ~$50-67/kg on 0.75-1 kg spools, specialist PA12 grades $55-90/kg. Precise current retail range unverified.

recommended: functional gears, bushings and low-friction bearings
tool handles, jigs and shop fixtures
end-use functional prototypes needing toughness and fatigue life
not_recommended: outdoor UV-exposed parts (degrades in sunlight)
dimensionally critical precision fits without post-print conditioning
humid-environment enclosures and wet-service parts
quick one-off prints (drying overhead outweighs the print)
parts under sustained load needing high stiffness and low creep
beginner projects on open-frame printers

filaments.name: PC (Polycarbonate)
filaments.summary: The high-temperature structural workhorse of desktop FDM: the best heat resistance, stiffness and sustained-load performance of the common materials, with impact toughness to match. The price is process difficulty — 250-310 °C nozzle temperatures, an enclosure that is effectively mandatory, and hygroscopy on par with nylon.

price.notes: 2025-2026 pricing for standard unfilled PC: Polymaker PolyMax PC $38.99/0.75 kg (~$52/kg) or $144.99/3 kg (~$48/kg); Bambu and other mainstream brands generally $30-45/kg. Precise low end unverified.

recommended: functional prototypes needing heat plus impact resistance
optically clear lens and light-guide parts on clear grades
not_recommended: food-contact items (standard grades are not food-safe)
quick low-effort prints (drying plus enclosure overhead)
fine-detail miniatures (high temperatures worsen stringing and detail)
long-term outdoor UV exposure without coating or stabiliser
beginner setups and open-frame printers

filaments.name: PCTG (Glycol-Modified PCT Copolyester)
filaments.summary: PETG's tougher, clearer, more expensive sibling: the same easy-going amorphous copolyester behaviour with markedly better impact strength, optical clarity, chemical resistance and near-isotropic layer bonding. The costs are a hotter nozzle (250-270 °C, all-metal hotend), more shrink-driven warp than PETG, and roughly double the price.

price.notes: Notably pricier than PETG: general market $30-45/kg, Fiberlogy around EUR 36/kg in Europe, Essentium around $53/kg in the US. The premium reflects a small number of CHDM raw-material suppliers and few filament makers offering the grade.

recommended: protective cases and enclosures needing impact toughness
mechanical parts exposed to solvents, oils or fuels
optically clear parts (better clarity than PETG)
outdoor parts needing yellowing resistance at moderate temperatures
snap-fit and living-hinge-adjacent parts leveraging ductility
not_recommended: high-temperature or near-boiling applications (HDT ~64-76 °C, softens near 80 °C)
parts needing maximum rigidity or stiffness (flexural modulus below PET and ABS)
structural loads applied along Z (standing impact collapses to ~1.5 kJ/m²)
budget or high-volume printing (cost and limited availability)
printers without a heated bed and an all-metal hotend

filaments.name: PET (Polyethylene Terephthalate)
filaments.summary: The unmodified parent of PETG: stiffer, more heat-tolerant and more chemically resistant, but semi-crystalline, so it shrinks and warps as it crystallises rather than simply cooling. That single difference makes it markedly harder to print than PETG and explains why it stayed a niche material even though it is the world's most common polyester.

price.notes: Standard PET runs roughly $20-35/kg. Recycled grades are similar or slightly cheaper — FormFutura ReForm rPET is around EUR 16.50/kg (~$18/kg), while branded rPET spools commonly sit at $25-35/kg.

recommended: parts needing more stiffness and thermal headroom than PETG
general-purpose functional parts where stiffness outranks ease of printing
not_recommended: first prints or beginner projects (warp-prone and needs tuning)
large flat parts without an enclosure (severe corner lift from crystallisation shrinkage)
tight-tolerance parts on open-frame printers in uncontrolled ambient conditions
long unattended prints (needs closer monitoring than PETG)
printers without a bed that reaches 70-90 °C or without an all-metal hotend

filaments.name: PETG (Glycol-Modified PET)
filaments.summary: The workhorse step up from PLA: tougher, far better layer adhesion, genuinely water-resistant and usable to ~70 °C, with only mild warp and no enclosure requirement. Pays for it with stringing, oozing, softer detail and supports that fuse hard to the part.

price.notes: 2025-2026 pricing for standard unfilled grades: budget $18-22, mid $22-26, premium $30-42 per kg. The historical price gap with ABS has closed — budget PETG now often matches or undercuts ABS.

recommended: outdoor brackets and enclosures (moderate UV exposure)
water bottles and non-potable liquid containment
parts where layer adhesion / Z-strength is critical
not_recommended: high-precision dimensional parts (more ooze and stringing than PLA)
parts with crisp overhangs or long bridges (sags and droops)
geometry needing easy support removal (supports fuse strongly)
under-hood or high-temperature applications (HDT ~68-80 °C)
fine-detail miniatures (glossy, stringy finish blurs detail)

filaments.name: PLA (Polylactic Acid)
filaments.summary: The default FDM material and the easiest polymer to print: no enclosure, almost no warp, excellent dimensional accuracy and the lowest emissions of the common filaments. The trade-off is heat and weather: parts soften near 55-60 °C, creep under sustained load, and embrittle in sunlight.

price.notes: 2025-2026 pricing for standard unfilled grades: budget $14-18, mid $18-22, premium/specialty $25-35 per kg

not_recommended: outdoor parts (UV embrittlement and discolouration)
sustained-load mechanical parts (creep)
anything in a hot car or near heat (softens above ~60 °C)
automotive/engine-bay parts
direct hot-liquid food contact
high-impact or drop-prone parts (brittle fracture)

filaments.name: PP (Polypropylene)
filaments.summary: The living-hinge and chemical-resistance specialist: light, flexible, fatigue-resistant and essentially waterproof, with the lowest density of the common filaments so a spool yields the most part volume. It is also one of the hardest materials to print — extreme warping and near-universal non-adhesion mean it needs its own build surface, since the same non-stick behaviour that makes PP tape a great release layer for other materials makes PP itself refuse to stick to anything.

price.notes: 2025-2026 standard PP filament: Fiberlogy PP around €51/kg (~$55/kg); 0.75-1 kg spools commonly $30-55 each on the wider market. Precise current USD range unverified.

recommended: living hinges for snap-together boxes and lids
parts subject to repeated flexing and fatigue
not_recommended: high-precision dimensional parts (severe warping and shrinkage)
rigid structural load-bearing parts (low strength and stiffness)
parts relying on out-of-box bed or support adhesion
glued or solvent-welded assemblies (PP resists most adhesives and solvents)
fine-detail miniatures (poor first-layer control on most surfaces)

filaments.name: PVA (Polyvinyl Alcohol)
filaments.summary: The classic water-dissolvable support material, used almost exclusively as the second extruder in multi-material prints rather than as a build material. It pairs best with PLA at similar print temperatures, but it is extremely hygroscopic: unprotected filament can absorb enough moisture in a couple of hours to clog, string, or fail mid-print.

price.notes: 2025-2026 pricing for standard unfilled grades. Budget brands (eSUN) sit at the low end, roughly $50-70/kg equivalent on 0.5 kg spools; premium brands (Prusament) reach or exceed the top of the range. Most PVA ships as 0.5 kg spools, so per-spool cost looks lower than per-kg.

filaments.name: PVB (Polyvinyl Butyral)
filaments.summary: A PLA-easy filament whose whole reason for existing is post-processing: brief exposure to isopropyl alcohol melts the layer lines into a glossy, near-glass finish, and the same solvent welds parts together seamlessly. In exchange it is brittle in Z, hygroscopic, heat-limited, and dissolves on contact with alcohol or many household cleaners.

price.notes: Roughly double standard PLA. Prusament PVB is $24.99 per 500 g spool (~$50/kg); the wider market sits around $33-45/kg.

recommended: artistic pieces intended for IPA vapour smoothing to a glass-like finish

not_recommended: structural or load-bearing parts (weak layer adhesion, brittle fracture)

outdoor parts (no UV stabilisation, low heat resistance)

filaments.name: TPE (Thermoplastic Elastomer)
filaments.summary: The softer, cheaper, more rubbery sibling of TPU: SEBS-based grades feel closer to real rubber, resist water and mild chemicals well, and several lines carry food and skin-contact certification. In exchange they are much weaker in tension than TPU, want very slow speeds with the fan off, and the 'TPE' label covers formulations different enough that datasheet numbers barely agree.

price.notes: Typically $25-45/kg (eSUN TPE-83A at $36.99/kg). Several sources note TPE runs slightly cheaper than equivalent TPU — 3D Insider describes eSUN Elastic TPE as a 'slightly less expensive alternative' to NinjaFlex TPU. Specialty and certified grades run higher; upper bound unverified.

recommended: phone and device cases and grips
wearable bands and straps with skin contact
not_recommended: structural or load-bearing parts
high-precision mechanical parts
applications above roughly 80 °C
parts needing high tensile strength (much weaker than TPU)
abrasion- or oil-exposed parts (SEBS is weaker here than polyester-based TPU)

filaments.name: TPU (Thermoplastic Polyurethane)
filaments.summary: The default flexible filament: a rubbery block copolymer that prints on any direct-drive machine at room temperature with essentially no warp, and absorbs impact and vibration that rigid filaments transmit. The difficulties are all in feeding and tuning — it buckles in Bowden paths, needs slow speeds and retraction work, drinks moisture, and is markedly weaker in Z than XY.

price.notes: 2025-2026 pricing for standard 85A-95A grades: budget generic ~$20-25, Bambu TPU ~$25-30, premium NinjaTek Cheetah and specialty soft grades $50-70+ per kg. Bounds unverified — flexible filament retail pricing is not consistently published per kilogram.

recommended: wearables such as watch bands and orthotic inserts
cable strain reliefs and protective sleeving
not_recommended: rigid structural or load-bearing parts
high-temperature applications
tight-tolerance mating parts (elastic recovery causes dimensional drift)
large flat parts (bed adhesion and removal are awkward)
food-contact use on uncertified grades

manufacturers.name: COEX LLC (COEX 3D)

manufacturers.name: colorFabb B.V.

manufacturers.name: DAS FILAMENT

manufacturers.name: Devil Design (Devil Design Sp. J.)

manufacturers.name: ELEGOO

manufacturers.name: Eryone (Shenzhen Eryone Technology Co., Ltd.)

manufacturers.name: Extrudr (FD3D GmbH)

manufacturers.name: Jayo
manufacturers.summary: Budget AliExpress/Amazon filament label sold through its own storefronts, positioned as a cheaper alternative to Sunlu-branded product. Jayo is not a factory: its filament is manufactured by Sunlu, so its material originates from Sunlu's Chinese production bases.

manufacturers.name: Keene Village Plastics (Village Plastics)
manufacturers.summary: Long-established US industrial plastics manufacturer that extruded its way into 3D printing filament at wholesale scale, self-describing as "the largest manufacturer of high-quality 3D printer filaments in the United States". Operates consumer-facing as Village Plastics and reached the hobbyist market by acquiring the MakeShaper filament brand in 2018/2019.

manufacturers.name: Kexcelled (North Bridge New Material Technology (Suzhou) Co., Ltd.)
manufacturers.summary: Suzhou-based filament and resin manufacturer selling directly under the Kexcelled brand, with an unusually strong certification profile for a value-priced Chinese producer (ISO 9001, ISO 13485 medical QMS, FDA and CE-MDR Class I, UL 94 V0 on select materials) and manufacturing diversified beyond China into Thailand.

manufacturers.name: Kimya (ARMOR Group)
manufacturers.summary: French engineering-filament brand of the ARMOR Group industrial group, positioned for functional end-use parts rather than hobbyist printing. Best documented product is ABS-R, an impact-modified ABS; the broader catalog reportedly spans PLA, PETG, TPU, nylon (including reinforced grades), PC and carbon/glass-fiber-filled engineering materials.

manufacturers.name: Kingroon (Kingroon 3D)
manufacturers.summary: Budget Chinese printer brand (KP3S, KLP1) that also sells a wide house filament catalog. Kingroon does not extrude its own filament: per owner-verified records it is manufactured by Landu in China, and a third-party review source independently characterises Kingroon filament as an OEM brand attached to the printers, corroborating the contract-manufacture pattern without naming Landu. Positioning is firmly budget, with bulk 10kg pricing and occasional batch-to-batch variability reported.

manufacturers.name: Landu (Hongkong Landu Innovations Technology Co., Limited)
manufacturers.summary: Hong Kong-registered filament company with large-scale production in Shenzhen and Dongguan — a 50,000 sq m manufacturing centre running roughly 3,000 tons per month. Sells budget-priced LANDU-branded filament, resin and accessories, and is the confirmed OEM behind Kingroon-branded filament.

manufacturers.name: MatterHackers, Inc.
manufacturers.summary: One of the largest US 3D-printing retailers, based in Lake Forest, California. MatterHackers is primarily a marketplace for third-party printers and materials — and owns/operates the LulzBot printer brand — but also sells house-brand filament under Pro Series (engineering tier) and MH Build Series (budget tier), claimed as made in the USA.

manufacturers.name: NinjaTek (Fenner Precision Polymers)
manufacturers.summary: Flexible-filament specialist operating as a division of Fenner Precision Polymers, part of Fenner (UK), which Michelin Group acquired in May 2018. Its catalog is almost entirely TPU — NinjaFlex, Chinchilla, Cheetah, Eel and Armadillo — extruded in the US on the back of Fenner's roughly 50 years of belt and polymer extrusion experience. It also retails colorFabb-branded materials through its own shop.

manufacturers.name: Overture 3D Technologies, LLC
manufacturers.summary: US-based consumer filament brand founded in 2019 and headquartered in Houston, Texas. Overture is an importer/brand rather than a factory: its filament is manufactured by Polymaker (project-owner verified), so the material itself originates in China. Best known as a high-volume Amazon budget/mid brand with a broad PLA aesthetic range.

manufacturers.name: Polymaker
manufacturers.summary: R&D-led filament manufacturer headquartered in Changshu, China, with offices in Shanghai, Utrecht and Houston. Its catalog spans budget aesthetic PLA (PolyTerra/Panchroma) through engineering composites (Fiberon, PolyMax), and it is one of very few Chinese-origin brands with confirmed US manufacturing capacity.

manufacturers.name: Protopasta (Protoplant, Inc.)
manufacturers.summary: Protoplant, Inc. (dba "Protoplant, makers of Protopasta") is a US specialty filament maker founded in 2013 via Kickstarter by Dustin Cram, Aaron Cram and Alexander Dick. It extrudes all of its own product in Vancouver, Washington and is best known as an early pioneer of composite and filled PLA rather than a broad engineering-material catalog.

manufacturers.name: Prusa Research a.s. (Prusament)
manufacturers.summary: Czech joint-stock company behind the Original Prusa printer ecosystem. Its filament brand, Prusament, is extruded in-house by wholly-owned subsidiary Prusa Polymers a.s. on roughly 12 production lines near Prague. Vertically integrated: Prusa makes its own filament, printers and build surfaces, and no evidence was found of it white-labelling for other brands.

manufacturers.name: Push Plastic
manufacturers.summary: US filament extruder established September 2013, running its own production since inception and claiming 25+ years of plastics experience behind it. Unusually broad engineering catalog for a small US operation — PEI, PMMA and PC+PBT alongside the commodity materials — in both 1.75 mm and 2.85 mm, with SAM.gov certification for government and institutional sales.

manufacturers.name: QIDI Tech (Zhejiang Qidi Technology Co., Ltd.)
manufacturers.summary: Chinese printer maker selling under the QIDI / Qidi Tech consumer brand, known for actively-heated-chamber machines (X-Max, Q1 series). Its filament is a house accessory line sold almost exclusively through qidi3d.com rather than third-party retail, and is profiled specifically for QIDI's own printers. No third-party OEM relationship is confirmed and the brand does not appear in the owner-verified ground-truth table, so whether production is truly in-house or contract-manufactured remains open.

manufacturers.name: Real Filament
manufacturers.summary: Dutch filament brand describing itself as 'a Dutch company that produces 3D filament within Europe'. Around eight filament types listed without distinct line branding - PLA (including a biodegradable/pliable variant), PETG, TPU, PVA, a water-soluble support and a 'multifunctional durable' material - sold from NL stock and through a reseller network in the Netherlands and UK.

manufacturers.name: ROSA3D (ROSA PLAST Sp. z o.o.)
manufacturers.summary: Polish filament manufacturer in Hipolitow near Warsaw, self-described as a 'Polish manufacturer of 3D printing filament'. Broad catalogue spanning PLA, PET-G (including a high-speed grade), PCTG, ABS, ASA, PC, TPU, PA (incl. PA12+CF), PP/PP-GF30, HIPS and an R-Series recycled range, with specialty ESD-safe, medical-grade and PTFE-infused grades.

manufacturers.name: Shenzhen Snapmaker Technologies Co., Ltd.
manufacturers.summary: Shenzhen company founded 2016, distinctive for building multi-function 3-in-1 machines (3D printing, laser, CNC) rather than printers alone (Snapmaker 2.0, Artisan, J1, U1). Filament is an in-house accessory line with RFID-tagged spools tuned to Snapmaker's own machines, and the material range is narrower than pure filament brands — PLA, PETG and TPU only, with no confirmed ABS/ASA/PA/PC lines. No third-party OEM relationship is documented and the brand is absent from the owner-verified ground-truth table.

manufacturers.name: Spectrum Filaments (Spectrum Group Sp. z o.o.)
manufacturers.summary: Polish filament manufacturer near Warsaw that debuted in 2015 and now lists 50+ materials, from commodity PLA and PET-G through PCTG, PA, PP, PC, PPS, PEBA and soluble supports, plus pellets and a spool refill system. States that all filament is produced in-house in Poland, and is expanding into North America with a dedicated US warehouse and store.

manufacturers.name: Sunlu (Zhuhai Sunlu Industrial Co., Ltd.)
manufacturers.summary: Founded July 2013 in Zhuhai, Guangdong, Sunlu is a high-volume Chinese filament producer with three FDM production bases, 20,000+ tons of cumulative shipments and 36 global distribution points. It sells under its own brand, is well known for its S-series filament dryers, and manufactures for several budget retail labels.

manufacturers.name: taulman3D
manufacturers.summary: One of the earliest specialty-nylon FDM filament brands, historically based in Missouri, USA, and known for Nylon 645, Nylon 680 FDA, Alloy 910, Nylon Bridge and the T-Glase copolyester line. Acquired by Brazilian petrochemical major Braskem, which now hosts the taulman3D catalog on its braskem3d.com additive-manufacturing portal alongside Braskem's own PP/PE and bio-based filaments.

manufacturers.name: Tinmorry
manufacturers.summary: Budget filament label distributed largely through Amazon and its own storefronts, emphasising metallic and silk specialty finishes alongside standard PLA and PETG. No legal entity or factory was identified; third-party reviews repeatedly flag batch-to-batch consistency problems.

manufacturers.name: UltiMaker (Ultimaker B.V.)
manufacturers.summary: Dutch desktop and professional FDM printer maker that also formulates and sells its own verified material range (Tough PLA, CPE/CPE+, Nylon, PC, TPU 95A, PVA, PP and more). Headquartered in Utrecht since 2019; the 2022 merger with MakerBot brought that brand in-house, leaving NPM Capital with 53.5% and Stratasys with 46.5%. Runs an open materials marketplace with third-party partners such as Tectonic-3D on top of its own catalog.

manufacturers.name: Voxelab
manufacturers.summary: Budget consumer sub-brand of Zhejiang Flashforge 3D Technology Co., Ltd., best known historically for the Aquila printer line. Voxelab is a label rather than an independent extruder: its filament is manufactured by Flashforge in China, a relationship that is owner-verified, self-disclosed on Voxelab's own about page, and even visible in the brand's Amazon storefront name ('Voxelab Official: Flashforge 3D Printer'). Manufacturing countries here therefore reflect Flashforge's Zhejiang facilities.

manufacturers.name: Ziro (ZIRO 3D Print Technology Company Limited)
manufacturers.summary: Hong Kong-registered brand with production in Shenzhen, differentiated by an unusually broad range of exotic and novelty aesthetic PLA finishes rather than engineering materials. Ziro also runs its own published OEM/private-label and wholesale programme, so it likely supplies unnamed third-party labels.

plates.name: Textured PEI (powder-coated spring steel)
plates.summary: The modern default build surface: powder-coated polyetherimide on flexible spring steel. Grips hot, releases cold, needs no adhesives for most materials, and leaves a uniform textured finish. Example entry pending Phase D research.
plates.surface_makeup: Polyetherimide (PEI) powder coating fused onto a spring-steel sheet
